subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Gravitational Microlensing
description: Learn Gravitational Microlensing in one minute.

hook.text: When a star with a planet passes in front of a background star, gravity bends the light and briefly magnifies it.

buildup.text: The planet creates an extra spike in the magnification curve. This method can find planets thousands of light-years away.

discovery.text: OGLE-2005-BLG-390Lb was found this way—a cold, distant world 21,000 light-years away, one of the farthest known.

twist.text: Microlensing events are one-time—they never repeat. You get one chance to observe each detection.

climax.text: NASA's Roman Space Telescope will use microlensing to detect thousands of exoplanets, including free-floating ones.

punchline.text: Gravity bends light. One brief flash reveals a hidden world. No second chances.

quiz.question: What is unique about gravitational microlensing detections?
options: They are one-time events that never repeat
They can only detect gas giant planets
They require the planet to transit its star

details.summary: Gravitational microlensing detects exoplanets when a foreground star's gravity bends light from a background star, and an orbiting planet creates a brief spike in the magnification pattern.
details.whyItMatters: Microlensing is the only current method that can detect planets at cosmological distances and rogue planets without host stars. It fills a unique niche in the exoplanet detection toolkit.
takeaways: Detects planets via brief spikes in gravitational lensing events
Can find planets at great distances and rogue planets
Each detection is a one-time, non-repeatable event

faq.question: How does microlensing reveal a planet?
faq.answer: When a foreground star lenses a background star, the brightening follows a smooth, predictable curve. If the foreground star has a planet, the planet's gravity adds a brief, sharp spike or dip to this curve. The spike's shape reveals the planet's mass and its distance from the host star.

faq.question: Why can't microlensing events be repeated?
faq.answer: Microlensing requires precise alignment of foreground and background stars as they move through the galaxy. Such alignments are random and extremely rare for any given pair of stars. Once the stars drift apart, the lensing event is over permanently — you can't go back and observe the planet again.
